entities.name: MGM Records
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
MGM Records, founded in 1946 as the recording arm of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer film studio, was one of the most significant American record labels of the mid-20th century, known for its Broadway cast albums, film soundtracks, and pop artists including Connie Francis and Eric Burdon. MGM Records' roster and releases bridged Hollywood's golden era film music with the popular music industry's transformation through rock and roll. The label was acquired by PolyGram in 1972 and eventually absorbed into Universal Music Group.

MGM Records' founding in 1946 reflected Hollywood studios' attempt to capture the profitable recording market during the LP era. The label released original Broadway cast albums including Oklahoma! and other Rodgers and Hammerstein recordings that are among the definitive documents of American musical theatre. The label's roster during the 1950s-1970s included artists across multiple genres: Hank Williams (country), Connie Francis (pop), and the Animals with Eric Burdon (British Invasion rock).

Hank Williams's MGM recordings (1947-1952) are among the most influential in country music history: 'Your Cheatin' Heart,' 'I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry,' and 'Lovesick Blues' defined country music's emotional language. Williams died on New Year's Day 1953 at 29, leaving behind recordings that influenced Bob Dylan, Bruce Springsteen, and virtually every country artist since. MGM Records' absorption into PolyGram and ultimately Universal Music demonstrates the music industry's consolidation from hundreds of independent labels to three global majors.
